title: Rotating lifts: What it should & shouldn't be
summary: NH explains how to rotate lifts properly. Rotations should be planned in the program, never done on a whim or triggered by stalling, and should stay within close variations. He describes his 8-day split with within-day rotations, warns against having too many lifts, and argues the law of accommodation can be beaten by changing volume and intensity instead of swapping lifts.

claims.claim: Rotating lifts means changing exercises within a program without changing the program as a whole; it should always be scheduled, not done by feel.
Lift rotation is an old practice that will likely be repopularised and bastardised on YouTube fitness for commercial reasons.
The belief that bodybuilders needn't follow specificity is naive; body-part splits should be the most advanced form of programming, not just 'Monday chest'.
You can't decide on the day to swap bench for weighted push-ups; a well-written hypertrophy program must be respected.
Rotation should never be triggered by stalling: you're running from failure, and gains on a new lift started at lower weight aren't real progress.
Swapping a 350 lb back squat for 135 lb safety bar squats loses huge tonnage and intensity; working the SSB back up to 350 isn't a gain, and the interim is junk volume.
When rotating lifts, match the weight. A technical new lift such as a specialty bar should be added alongside the old one and only replace it once it's heavy enough.
Scheduled rotations should have a reason; arbitrary 6-week blocks can force you off a lift you're still progressing on, and repeatedly reset you just as progress starts.
His alternative: small rotations within an 8-day body-part split, where lifts never leave the program and he picks which to do based on the week, so each is done every 10-12 days.
A lift done only every 15 days or monthly wastes time: you keep relearning it, building neural adaptation rather than the muscle damage needed for hypertrophy.
Keep rotations among close variations (e.g. close-grip vs regular bench); dips and bench are too different to share a rotation, so rotate dips with pause dips.
Don't be greedy in programming: wanting 45 lifts leads to a messy catalogue of lifts going in and out, or picked at random on the day.
You can pick from a short list of triceps exercises, but choosing randomly on the day is too much freedom.
The law of accommodation (progress stalls on a familiar lift) can be bypassed by changing volume, intensity or supersets rather than dropping the lift.
